references.text: The same command not to oppress foreigners, with the same justification regarding Israel's experience in Egypt.
An expanded law concerning the treatment of foreigners, including the command to love them as oneself, referencing Egypt.
A command to love the foreigner because the Israelites themselves were foreigners in Egypt.
Prohibition against perverting justice for the foreigner, with a reminder of slavery in Egypt.
A curse upon anyone who perverts justice for foreigners.
The prophet Jeremiah warns against oppressing foreigners, fatherless children, and widows.
Ezekiel condemns the oppression of foreigners in Israel.
An accusation against the people for oppressing foreigners and the poor.
Zechariah exhorts not to oppress widows, fatherless children, foreigners, or the poor.
The Lord will testify against those who oppress foreigners.
An exhortation to hospitality, with reference to welcoming strangers.
This version confirms and consolidates the law's fundamental principle of empathy based on shared history.
Applies the principle of empathy even toward former oppressors (the Egyptians), deepening the understanding of the law's breadth.
Connects the law's demand for justice toward foreigners directly to the commandment of love and God's own nature.
Fulfills and deepens the law's requirements by identifying the foreigner with Christ himself.
Expresses the very prohibition against oppression in the same law book as the theological justification (candidate 3).
